key_insight: A broad humanoid controller can often solve new loco-manipulation tasks without retraining if its existing skills are exposed through a richer planning-to-control interface. By letting the system improve from its own attempts at test time, the paper shows that latent competence can be repurposed and retained for contact-rich, multi-stage behaviors.
problem_solved: The paper addresses how to make humanoid robots perform new loco-manipulation tasks that they were never explicitly trained for, without expensive retraining or task-specific redesign.
method: Use test-time evolution to adapt behavior from the robot's own rollouts rather than offline retraining.
Represent tasks through reward programs that connect high-level planning with low-level control in a way that can express contact-rich, multi-stage interactions.
Iteratively refine the reward/programming signal so the controller reuses existing skills and retains useful improvements across attempts.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a path to more scalable robot adaptation: robots can tackle new tasks at deployment time using pre-existing capabilities instead of requiring full retraining. It also points to a practical way to bridge planning and control for complex humanoid manipulation.

paper_title: InterEvolve: Test-Time Evolution of Reward Programs for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
paper_authors: Zhuo Lin, Sirui Xu, Liuyu Bian, Yu-Xiong Wang, Liang-Yan Gui
